narratives.Description: Today either root flag file turns Directive off for any process that can create it, and the only stop is the #6136 plant guard, which reads shell command text. This story makes a bare disable flag turn nothing off on every reader it ships: the temporary off switch becomes a plain-line record that `kill-switch:on` writes into the payload root `.deft/authz/` store after the kept terminal mint, bound to `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir`, and `kill-switch:off` removes it with `--confirm` and no mint. The core detector, runtime hook dispatch, launcher entry guard, deposited outer hook and git-hook helper (shell only, no Node) apply one exact whole-line record contract with shared fixtures, and each prints one warning on a bare flag. The outer hook passes a reader flag and the git-hook helper carries a marker that doctor reports. A later slice adds a host-hook-only break-glass variable with an expiry date at most 7 days ahead, and a last slice makes the opt-out flag change no decision in an installed checkout and puts the mint on `policy:disable-directive`. The plant guard stays unchanged; retiring it is #7065. This is hardening, not human-only authority.
narratives.Overview:
1. Claim. A bare flag file no longer turns anything off on the readers this issue ships. The off switch is as strong as the grant store and the kept mint, no stronger: the mint refuses shells with agent or CI markers and non-interactive callers; a pseudo-terminal with markers unset passes it; store-guard holes (#6292, #6981, #7034, #7036, paths built at run time, programmatic writes) let an agent write a record, as they let it forge the settings grant that already authorizes a plant. Docs, criteria and messages never say agents cannot turn Directive off.
2. Disable record. `kill-switch:on` (name open) runs `refuseNonInteractiveMint`, refuses under an active UAT lease, and atomically publishes `.deft/authz/kill-switch.disable` in the payload root's store as plain lines: `schema=deft.kill-switch.v1`, `gitDir=<output of git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir>`, `mintedAt=…`, `mintedVia=…`. `kill-switch:off` deletes only that file with `--confirm` and no mint (re-enabling tightens, #5980); the issue's second criterion changes to match. Full re-enable still needs a new agent session.
3. One reader contract. A record counts only when it is a regular file (not a link) that contains the exact whole line `schema=deft.kill-switch.v1` and the exact whole line `gitDir=` followed by what `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` prints at check time. Other lines are display only. Whole-line exact matching needs no escaping, so the shell (`grep -qxF`) and Node readers agree; line-ending and git-output handling are fixed in the shared fixtures. Anything else leaves enforcement on with one bounded warning. The binding isolates checkouts against copies; it does not prove freshness or who wrote it. Named limits: restoring saved record bytes after off, and a checkout used from both Git for Windows and WSL git (one mint each). One shared fixture set runs against every reader.
4. Readers and warning. The core detector (dispatcher, `session:start`, SessionStart hook, doctor), the runtime hook dispatch, the launcher entry guard and the deposited outer hook (`node:fs` plus `git`) apply item 3. The git-hook helper applies it with shell tests, `git` and `grep -qxF` before it looks for the runtime or `node`, where it checks the flag today (`.githooks/_directive-run.sh` 12-19), so git-hook stand-down still needs no Node. A bare disable flag is ignored by all of them; every hook event they serve prints one warning naming the file and the on verb; doctor and `session:start` print it too, and print an existing record's `mintedVia` and `mintedAt`. A tracked flag still never disables.
5. Reader flag, marker and migration. The new outer hook passes `--kill-switch-reader v1` to the runtime hook binary (`host-hook-outer.ts` 333, `hook-dispatch.ts` 319 parser), and the runtime accepts it; a new outer hook reaching an older runtime fails closed as a hook failure (named). The new git-hook helper carries a marker line. Doctor reports a host-hook call without the reader flag, and a checkout-local helper (`<show-toplevel>/.githooks/_directive-run.sh`, the file the entry scripts source) without the marker, and names `directive upgrade` or `install --repair`. The flag and the marker are compatibility information only, never authority, and they are the inputs #7065 builds on. Update, refresh and repair do not refuse on an opt-out flag that item 7 ignores. Docs, the recovery message and the agents-entry line (then `task agents:refresh`) say presence alone means nothing on current readers and Directive reports when it is off. No auto-mint for an existing flag. Installer-side touches (polfer's area, named): the outer hook and its flag, the git-hook helper and its marker, the launcher check, doctor's status, redeposit, and the refresh and repair refusal.
6. Break-glass variable (name open). Host hook processes honor it always (the outer hook, including when the runtime is missing, and the runtime hook path); git hooks and CLI verbs never do, so a prefixed command cannot use it and those keep enforcing; `session:start` and doctor report it. Every honored event prints a banner naming the variable. Its value is an expiry date at most 7 days ahead; a past, unparsable or further-out value is ignored with a warning, so a committed value goes stale. Doctor flags the variable's name in tracked host config files. Named limits, same class as rewriting hook registration: an agent can start a nested host with it set, a tracked host config `env` block sets it for every clone, and `setx` or a shell profile sets it for the next launch.
7. Opt-out parity. A checkout counts as installed when `package.json` has an exact runtime pin (`readPin`, `packages/core/src/resolution/pin.ts` 120), or a Directive outer hook is registered for any host, or the Directive git-hook helper is present, or a legacy `.deft/core` exists; a missing `node_modules` never makes an installed checkout count as uninstalled. In an installed checkout the opt-out flag changes no hook, `session:start`, refresh or repair decision; doctor reports the inconsistency and init keeps refusing. In an uninstalled checkout it keeps today's meaning: it stops install offers and wins over org force-on. `policy:disable-directive` runs `refuseNonInteractiveMint` before it writes the flag (today it is allowed outside UAT); in an installed checkout it does not print "disabled" but says the flag records the preference and changes no enforcement while Directive is installed; `policy:enable-directive` stays free. There is no opt-out record, so the free off verb cannot remove one. No network or ref read.
8. Plant guard stays. The #6136 plant guard (shell mention rule, its glob test and the always-on plant gate) stays in force in every checkout, unchanged. Retiring it is #7065, gated on a migration step that removes old outer hooks and git-hook helpers or makes them read the record or fail closed, with the four old-reader paths the audits found as its bar.
9. Order: items 1-5 first, then 6, then 7. Each may be its own PR under #6740.
10. Tests: record present (off); bare flag (on, warning); malformed, linked or copied record, or one from another checkout (on, warning); off without a mint; on refuses in an agent-marked or non-terminal shell and under UAT; the git-hook helper stands down on a valid record with no `node` on PATH and no `node_modules`, and ignores the variable; the outer hook honors the record and the variable with no `node_modules`; variable with a near future date (host hooks off, banner), a past date or one more than 7 days ahead (on, warning), and ignored by a CLI verb; doctor reports a call without the reader flag and an unmarked checkout-local helper; the plant guard still refuses a shell plant of the disable flag after items 1-7 ship; installation cases: exact pin with no `.deft/core`, the same with `node_modules` absent, a legacy deposit, and an unconfigured project, where only the last keeps the opt-out flag's old meaning; `policy:disable-directive` refuses without a mint and, in an installed checkout, does not print "disabled".

## Acceptance Criteria

- A bare disable flag file turns nothing off on any reader this issue ships; every hook event they serve, doctor and `session:start` print one warning naming the file and the on verb.
- `kill-switch:on` refuses without the kept mint and under UAT, and writes the plain-line record bound to `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir`; `kill-switch:off` removes it with `--confirm` and no mint.
- Every reader (core, runtime, launcher, outer hook, git-hook helper) applies one exact whole-line record contract with shared fixtures; the git-hook helper does it without `node`; invalid, copied or other-checkout records leave enforcement on.
- The outer hook passes a reader flag and the git-hook helper carries a marker; doctor reports calls without the flag and an unmarked checkout-local helper and names the redeposit; the #6136 plant guard stays in force unchanged.
- The break-glass variable turns off host hooks only, needs an unexpired date at most 7 days ahead, prints a banner, and is ignored by git hooks and CLI verbs; doctor flags it in tracked host configs.
- In a checkout installed by pin, deposited hooks or legacy deposit, the opt-out flag changes no hook, `session:start`, refresh or repair decision; in an uninstalled one it keeps today's meaning; `policy:disable-directive` needs the mint and does not print "disabled" in an installed checkout.
- The kill-switch and opt-out docs, the recovery message and the agents-entry line describe the verbs, the variable, the warning and the honest limits, and the "create the file" step is removed.
- Tests cover each case in Bound remedy item 10.

narratives.UserStory: As an operator of a Directive checkout, I want the temporary off switch to be a minted record bound to this checkout instead of a bare flag file, so that an agent cannot turn Directive off by creating a file and I can still turn it off on purpose.

The outer hook (also when the runtime is missing) and the runtime hook path honor it and print a banner; git hooks and CLI verbs never do; session:start and doctor report it; doctor flags its name in tracked host config files. Tests: packages/core/src/policy/break-glass-variable.test.ts, packages/core/src/init-deposit/host-hook-outer.test.ts. Fragment changelog.d/6740-break-glass-variable.md.

Slice 3: opt-out parity and mint on policy:disable-directive (clauses 7, 16).

In an installed checkout the opt-out flag changes no hook, session:start, refresh or repair decision (packages/core/src/policy/no-deft-directive.ts, dispatcher.ts, session-start.ts, session-start-hook.ts, packages/runtime/src/session-start.ts, packages/core/src/init-deposit/refresh.ts, packages/core/src/hooks/cursor-plan-choice/adapter.ts, packages/core/src/policy/org-force-on-migration.ts); doctor reports the inconsistency and init keeps refusing (packages/core/src/init-deposit/init-dispatch.ts). ## In plain English
Directive has two root file flags that turn it off. The disable flag is a temporary test switch: an untracked regular file at the root makes every hook, the session ritual, the git hooks and the launcher stand down. The opt-out flag is the permanent "this project does not use Directive" marker. Any process that can create either file can turn Directive off. The only stop today is the #6136 plant guard, which reads the text of each shell command and refuses one that names a flag. Three arcs on that guard have halted with a new bypass found at every audit (#6959, #6982, #6981), and some forms can never be seen by reading text: names built at run time, a copy of an existing flag by wildcard, a copy of a whole directory. The opt-out flag can also be written by `policy:disable-directive`, which no guard stops outside a UAT lease.

#6740 proposes that a flag file alone does nothing. Directive is off only when a record that a person minted at a terminal sits in a protected store, or when the shell that launched the agent host set a break-glass variable. Once both flags work that way, the text-reading guard has nothing left to protect. The design questions are which store, how a record is tied to one checkout, what the terminal mint does and does not prove, who can set the variable, what the opt-out flag means for projects that commit it, how existing users migrate, and what happens to the guard.

## Operator decisions (Scott, recorded as constraints)
- "Arc #6740 now" (2026-11-22, relayed by the coordinator), after this framing: #6740 is the structural fix that would retire the plant-guard whack-a-mole; #6959 and #6982 are parked behind it; it builds right after #7031 and #6981.
- Run posture: design critique only; no ingest, promote or build from this arc.
- Goal from #6937 and #7031: fewer gates. #5980 records the principle that turning a protection off takes a human mint while tightening or re-enabling stays free.

## Pains
- P1 — A planted disable flag turns enforcement off. An untracked regular file at the root disables enforcement in every surface that checks it, and the only stop is a guard that reads command text. Its known holes are open on #6959, #6982, #6981, #6708 and #6292, and runtime-built names, wildcard copies of an existing flag and whole-directory copies are outside what text reading can see.
- P2 — The opt-out flag has the same hole. With a deposit present, the opt-out flag skips the SessionStart hook and the plan-choice adapter, makes `session:start` return disabled, makes install and upgrade fail closed, and tells agents through AGENTS.md and the setup skill that Directive is off. `policy:disable-directive` writes it from any shell: its command is classified `settings`, which is allowed while UAT is inactive, and the plant guard does not fire because the command does not name the file. #6740's criteria cover only the disable flag.

## Anchors at the dispatch SHA
- `packages/core/src/policy/deft-directive-disable.ts` 257-287: the detector; active when the file is a regular file (lstat, not a link) that `git ls-files` reports untracked.
- `packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts` 4791-4822: the disable flag short-circuits every hook event before any gate. 4880-4898: the opt-out flag short-circuits SessionStart only. 2120-2205: the #6136 plant gate (shell mention or Write/Edit basename), re-evaluated under a synthetic UAT lease so a human-origin `settings` grant still lets a plant through.
- `packages/core/src/init-deposit/host-hook-outer.ts` 203-226 and 318-326: the deposited outer hook uses Node built-ins only and checks the disable flag before it looks for the runtime (#5809). `.githooks/_directive-run.sh` 12-19 does the same in POSIX sh. `packages/cli/src/entry-guard.ts` 148-181: the launcher's copy. `packages/runtime/src/hook-dispatch.ts` 459-468: the runtime's copy.
- `packages/core/src/session/session-start.ts` 2293-2352: both flags stop `session:start`.
- `packages/core/src/policy/no-deft-directive.ts` 1-15 and 77-92: the opt-out flag is presence-only, wins locally over org force-on, and flag plus deposit is "inconsistent".
- `packages/runtime/src/policy.ts` 820-858: `policy:disable-directive` and `enable-directive` create and remove the opt-out flag with no terminal mint. 753-767: `policy:disable-host-hooks` (confirm only).
- `packages/core/src/authz/classify.ts` 187-218: policy mutators are `settings` (denied only under UAT); the two flag basenames.
- `packages/core/src/authz/evaluate.ts` 308-336 and 363-399: Write/Edit into `.deft/authz/` or `.deft/approved-scope/` is denied always, with no grant escape; shell writes are found by the text classifier. `packages/core/src/authz/protected-dest-realpath.ts` 20-32: the protected set.
- `packages/runtime/src/human-presence-mint.ts` 17-65 and 279-363: the terminal mint checks agent and CI environment markers, a TTY on stdin and stdout, a controlling terminal, `--confirm` and a typed `mint`. 191-207: no mint under an active UAT lease.
- `packages/core/src/init-deposit/gitignore.ts`: `.deft/authz/` and the disable flag are ignored per clone.
- `content/templates/agents-entry.md` 10: "check root disable flag (presence = flag). If present, stop DD load". Docs: `content/docs/deft-directive-disable.md` (Consumer note: create the file), `content/docs/no-deft-directive.md` (commit the flag).
- Probe (parent, measured, not a test): `classifyHookAuthzOps` plus `evaluateAuthzMutation` run with tsx on core source at 65fc6f74 (authz and policy sources identical to the dispatch SHA; `git diff --stat` empty), UAT inactive: `deft policy:disable-directive` gives `settings` and allow; `deft policy:disable-host-hooks --host claude --confirm` gives no op; `printf '%s\n' .deft/authz/grants/g | xargs touch` gives `settings` and allow (a #6292 form still open); `cp -r ../other/.deft .` gives no op; a store path built from a variable gives no op. `cd .deft/authz/grants && cp ~/f g` is now denied.

## Recommended mechanism (the thing to critique)
- R1. Kill record. A verb (name open, for example `deft kill-switch:on`) runs `refuseNonInteractiveMint` and refuses under an active UAT lease. It writes `.deft/authz/kill-switch.json` at the payload root through the containment writer: `{schema: "deft.kill-switch.v1", kind: "disable", root: <realpath of the payload root>, gitDir: <absolute git dir>, mintedAt, mintedVia, actor}` (actor is display only). The store is the one every authz grant lives in: ignored per clone, Write/Edit denied always, shell writes refused by the store classifier.
- R2. Off. `kill-switch:off` removes the record with `--confirm` and no mint, because re-enabling only tightens (#5980). This departs from acceptance criterion 2 ("terminal-only"). A new agent session is still needed for full re-enable.
- R3. One honor rule for every surface. Directive is off when the variable (R5) is set, or when a valid record exists: a regular file, not a link, that parses, has the schema, and whose `root` and `gitDir` match this checkout, so a record copied from another checkout does not count. Surfaces: core detector (dispatcher, `session:start`, SessionStart hook, doctor), runtime hook dispatch, launcher entry guard, the deposited outer hook and the git-hook helper. The last three cannot import core, so the record must be checkable with `node:fs` plus `git` (and sh for the git hook).
- R4. Bare file. A disable flag with no valid record is ignored. Every hook event prints one warning naming the file and the `kill-switch:on` verb; doctor and `session:start` print it too. A tracked flag still never disables.
- R5. Break-glass variable (name open, for example `DEFT_DIRECTIVE_OFF=1`). Read by the outer hook before the runtime check, by the runtime hook path, and shown by `session:start` and doctor. Not read by git hooks or by CLI verbs, since an agent can prefix its own command with it. Every event prints a banner naming the variable. Who can set it: whoever launches the agent host; hook processes inherit the host's environment and an agent's tool shell cannot change a running host's environment. Named limit: an agent can write files that set it for the next launch (a host config `env` block such as `.claude/settings.json`, a shell profile, `setx`), the same class as rewriting the host's hook registration, which Directive does not guard today.
- R6. Opt-out parity. With a deposit present, the opt-out flag counts only when it is tracked at the fetched default-branch tip (a merged project decision, as #2926 asks) or an opt-out record exists (R1 with `kind: "opt-out"`). A working-tree-only or branch-only opt-out flag is ignored with the same warning. With no deposit, presence keeps today's meaning: there is nothing to turn off, and it only stops install offers. When honored, the flag still wins over org force-on. `policy:disable-directive` mints the opt-out record; `policy:enable-directive` stays free.
- R7. Migration. Rewrite the kill-switch and opt-out docs, the recovery message, the agents-entry line (then `task agents:refresh`) and AGENTS.md. Do not auto-mint for an existing flag on upgrade; doctor names the verb. Installer-side touches (polfer's area, kept minimal and named): the deposited outer hook and git-hook helper change their first step from the flag to the record plus the variable and redeposit through `directive upgrade` or `install --repair`; the launcher's `isDisableFlagActive`; doctor's disabled status. Hosts that plant the flag before launch (#5133, held) move to the variable.
- R8. Plant guard. In the release where both flags need a record, retire the shell mention rule and its glob test and the always-on plant gate, and keep the protected-store guard. #6959, #6982 and #6708 then close as moot. Keep the gitignore line.
- R9. Tests: record present (off); bare file only (on, warning); record copied from another checkout (on, warning); variable set (off, banner); both verbs refuse in a non-terminal or agent shell; the off verb works without a mint; opt-out tracked at the default-branch tip honored, working-tree-only ignored with a deposit and honored without one; `policy:disable-directive` refuses without a mint; outer hook and git-hook helper honor the record and the variable with no runtime installed.

## Out of scope (named, not pains)
- `policy:disable-host-hooks` followed by `directive install --repair`, which removes the hook wiring and is a sanctioned agent-run recovery (#3785, #4854), and direct edits of host hook registration or the runtime's own files: the hook-wiring integrity class.
- The store guard's own holes: #7036 (a linked worktree writing the main clone's `.deft/authz/` by absolute path), #6981 (PowerShell tool), #7034 (terminal MCP tool), #6292. This arc should say which of them gate the claim.
- The WebAuthn approval (#6945, #7046) that later replaces the terminal mint.

## Questions for the critics
1. Refutation target: does R1-R4 make a planted disable flag harmless? Attack at least the store guard's holes, a copied record, a terminal mint driven through a pseudo-terminal with markers unset, a linked worktree, and a mixed-version window in which an old deposited outer hook still honors the bare file.
2. Store: `.deft/authz/` or a new protected folder? For a linked worktree, the payload root's store or the main clone's?
3. Can the built-ins-only outer hook, the launcher and a sh git hook check the record (R3)? Is the `root`/`gitDir` binding needed, and is it portable on Windows?
4. Off without a mint (R2) against acceptance criterion 2: which is right?
5. Variable (R5): honored always, or only when the runtime cannot reach a decision? Is excluding git hooks and CLI verbs right? Is the next-launch limit acceptable as named?
6. Opt-out (R6): is "tracked at the fetched default-branch tip, or a minted record; no deposit keeps today's meaning" faithful to #2926 (commit it; it wins locally over org force-on)? What happens offline or with no remote?
7. Guard (R8): retire in the same release, shrink, or keep as defence in depth? Can #6959, #6982 and #6708 close?
8. Honest claim: today a human-origin `settings` grant in `.deft/authz/` already authorizes a plant, so the kill switch already depends on the store guard. Is "one route instead of two" a fair statement of what R1-R8 buys, given the terminal mint proves presence, not identity?
9. Slices and gates: one PR, or (a) record, verbs, detector, variable and docs, (b) opt-out parity, (c) guard retirement? Name every new refusal, prompt or network read.

## In plain English

Directive currently lets a local flag turn off its protections. Moving that decision to a structured record would make a bare flag ineffective in updated readers, but the recommended mechanism does **not** establish that only a human can turn Directive off. An agent can still reach the record through gaps in the store guard, and terminal checks do not authenticate a human. The design cannot bind with its present human-only claim or unconditional guard retirement.

Answers to the nine questions:

1. **R1–R4:** A bare flag becomes harmless only after every reader changes. A forged record, a replayed same-checkout record, a mint driven through a pseudo-terminal, cross-worktree writes and old outer hooks remain counterexamples to the broader claim.
2. **Store:** Reuse `.deft/authz/` at the payload root. A new folder adds no security. A main-clone store would enlarge the authority and concurrency boundary unnecessarily.
3. **Readers and binding:** Node built-ins plus Git can check the proposed JSON without the installed runtime. A POSIX shell alone cannot robustly parse arbitrary JSON; the git helper needs a runtime-independent Node reader or another explicitly specified format. Root/git-directory binding prevents accidental cross-checkout reuse, not forgery or same-checkout replay. Windows canonicalization needs one shared specification.
4. **Off:** Re-enabling without a mint is appropriate for this checkout-local switch. It needs an explicit change to acceptance criterion 2, a reachable recovery path and truthful new-session messaging.
5. **Variable:** An unconditional, inherited **host-hook bypass** is clearer than an error-dependent bypass. Excluding CLI enforcement and git hooks is appropriate. It is not a full Directive-off switch, and next-launch manipulation is an accepted limitation only if stated as such.
6. **Opt-out:** R6 changes #2926’s local presence semantics. A remote-tracking ref is not proof of a human-approved merge. Offline, stale-ref and no-remote behavior are unspecified; fetching on hook events would be inappropriate.
7. **Guard:** Retirement should be a separate, conditional step after both flags and all deployed readers change. The named issues cannot close merely because the new record ships.
8. **Honest claim:** “Removes bare-file authority and consolidates local disable state” is defensible. “One route instead of two” needs qualification: the variable and default-ref opt-out introduce additional authority routes. The terminal test establishes terminal conditions, not human presence or identity.
9. **Slices:** The smallest useful first slice is a checkout-local record, on/off verbs, all temporary-disable readers, migration diagnostics and docs, explicitly sold as hardening rather than human-only authorization. Break-glass host behavior, permanent opt-out semantics and guard retirement deserve separate decisions. New stops comprise the on-mint checks, active-UAT refusal, `--confirm` and typed phrase; off requires only confirmation. Record rejection should leave enforcement active. Opt-out minting adds the same stops. No network read is necessary for the first slice; R6’s freshness requirement must be resolved separately.

A stronger human-only guarantee requires an authorization boundary the agent cannot reproduce or rewrite. Moving the file or extending the command-text classifier does not supply that boundary.

### 1. blocks-the-design — The protected store moves the plant target without establishing its authority

**Evidence:** At `b225dfde2eec95d4c1cc1d0a3e081591362451c8`, `packages/core/src/authz/evaluate.ts:329–399` denies recognized protected writes but allows ordinary mutations while UAT is inactive. `packages/core/src/authz/classify.ts:5981–6024` applies shell classification only to recognized shell tools and otherwise can return no operation. `packages/core/src/hooks/tools.ts:41–49` excludes PowerShell and terminal MCP tools. `packages/core/src/authz/protected-dest-realpath.ts:34–71` explicitly excludes destinations outside the payload root.

**Failure mode:** R1’s record has no authenticated provenance. A writer reaching the store through an uninspected tool can construct the schema, root and git-directory fields itself. A linked-worktree writer targeting another checkout is outside the cited realpath guard’s boundary. A containment writer constrains the official writer; it does not make that writer exclusive.

The command-text problem also remains inside the store guard: `classify.ts:5140–5190` recognizes redirects and selected writer/path combinations. Moving authority from a flag to JSON does not remove runtime-built paths or indirect writes.

**Disposition:** R1–R4 cannot support “only a human mints effective disable authority.” #6981, #7034, #7036 and #6292 bear directly on that claim, even if their implementations remain separate. Closing those known holes would improve coverage, but would not prove arbitrary shell execution cannot write the store. The first slice can honestly claim bare-file hardening; a stronger claim needs independently protected authorization.

### 2. blocks-the-design — The terminal mint can be automated without forging the record

**Evidence:** `packages/runtime/src/human-presence-mint.ts:22–65` lists environment markers; `279–363` checks those markers, TTY status, a controlling terminal, `--confirm` and the fixed phrase `mint`. Active UAT is separately refused at `191–207`.

**Shell fact, from my own knowledge rather than an executed probe:** A process able to create a child with a chosen environment can omit agent markers. On systems permitting pseudo-terminals, a controller can supply a controlling terminal and write the expected phrase through it. This does not require modifying Directive.

**Failure mode:** With UAT inactive, an automated caller satisfying those conditions uses the legitimate writer to produce the exact record R3 accepts. The record’s `actor`, `mintedVia` and timestamp do not distinguish that invocation from a person’s.

**Disposition:** Neither “human-only” nor “proves presence, not identity” accurately describes this check. Its defensible claim is that marked agent/CI shells and noninteractive invocations are refused. Retaining the mint as friction is reasonable and consistent with the supplied #7031 lean; treating it as authentication is not. A trusted approval mechanism would change this verdict only if its enrollment and verification boundary also resist agent substitution.

### 3. blocks-the-design — Default-branch tracking is not approval provenance

**Evidence:** The supplied #2926 body recommends committing the opt-out flag but defines local presence as authority. The pinned `packages/core/src/policy/no-deft-directive.ts:1–14,77–91` implements that local decision. R6 substitutes “tracked at the fetched default-branch tip.”

**Git facts, from my own knowledge:** Remote-tracking refs are mutable local refs. Their names do not authenticate their origin or prove a review or merge occurred. They can also be absent or stale offline.

**Failure mode:** A locally fabricated default-branch ref containing the opt-out flag satisfies a reader that checks only the ref’s tree. An authentic but stale ref can preserve opt-out after upstream removal. A no-remote repository has no defined result. These are distinct from the protected-record path.

**Disposition:** R6 cannot describe this condition as a verified merged project decision. It needs either an explicitly weaker trusted-local-Git assumption or a separately defined authority mechanism. The smallest first slice should avoid adding this route. Permanent opt-out parity remains necessary before claiming P2 relief or retiring the two-flag guard.

### 4. blocks-the-design — Updating the runtime does not update the first decision-maker

**Evidence:** `packages/core/src/init-deposit/host-hook-outer.ts:318–335` honors the existing flag before locating or invoking the runtime. `.githooks/_directive-run.sh:12–20` similarly returns before the runtime check. `packages/cli/src/entry-guard.ts:173–180` has another independent detector. Core’s early return is at `packages/core/src/hooks/dispatcher.ts:4791–4822`.

**Failure mode:** A new runtime can reject bare flags perfectly while an old deposited outer hook allows the request without invoking it. Installing a new package version is therefore insufficient. - A bare disable flag file turns nothing off on any surface; every hook event, doctor and `session:start` print one warning naming the file and the on verb.

Today any process that creates `.deft-directive-disable` turns Directive off (#3039). Guarding that against agent plants means classifying every shell command that could create the file, and names built at runtime (variables, sed, base64) cannot be seen by any static check. The kill switch should take effect only when a human mints it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A terminal-only verb turns the kill switch on after a typed confirmation, and writes the kill record into a Directive protected store; agent and CI shells refuse it.
- [ ] A matching terminal-only verb turns the kill switch off and removes the record.
- [ ] Hooks honor the kill switch only when a valid kill record exists in the protected store.
- [ ] A `.deft-directive-disable` file without a valid kill record is ignored, and every hook event prints one warning naming the file and the verb that turns the kill switch on.
- [ ] An environment variable set in the shell that launches the agent host disables Directive without any `deft` verb, for use when Directive itself is broken.
- [ ] The kill-switch docs (#3039) describe the verbs, the environment variable and the warning, and the old "create the file" step is removed.
- [ ] Tests cover: kill record present (disabled), bare file only (enabled, with the warning), environment variable set (disabled), and the verbs refusing in a non-terminal shell.

Refs #3039, #6681, #6708
